Chapter 3. The Demands of Perfection: Art, Politics, and Personal Growth.
Life at the academy? It’s a nonstop balancing act—like walking a tightrope with your heart in your throat.
Chasing artistic excellence isn’t just about perfecting your craft. Every lesson, every performance, gets tangled up with politics.
The students are reminded, day in and day out, that their talent isn’t really theirs. It belongs to the nation... to the revolution. That pressure to fit in, to always measure up, is enormous.
The teachers? Many have survived tough times themselves. They’re not just mentors—they’re also the ones making sure the rules are followed. They push everyone hard, demanding nothing less than perfection in every move.
Here, mistakes feel bigger than just messing up a step. They’re treated like betrayals—not just of yourself, but of the whole group. And the fear of letting everyone down? That’s always lurking in the background.
But even in this rigid system, moments of real artistry shine through. The boy starts to fall in love with dance itself—the way it can express emotion, tell stories, and reach across boundaries. He realizes that, even when art is boxed in by politics, it still has the power to rise above.
Friendships at the academy run deep. They’re shaped by both comfort and competition. Everyone shares everything—meals, secrets, dreams, disappointments. They cheer for each other’s wins and share the sting of failure. These bonds are forged in the heat of shared struggle.
As time passes, the boy’s skills sharpen. He learns how to hide his doubts, putting on a confident face for the world to see. The discipline that once felt suffocating now feels natural. Little by little, he earns roles in performances, and with each one, he gains respect—from both his peers and his teachers.
The applause from the audience? That’s a rush like nothing else. It’s one of the few moments where praise feels real.
But there’s a steep price to pay. Injuries are everywhere, and the fear of falling behind never really goes away. Everyone knows their place at the academy isn’t promised. One wrong move, one sign of weakness, and you could be out. That pressure to succeed—it’s relentless.
Beyond the academy walls, the whole country is shifting. Political campaigns come and go, each bringing new slogans, new rules, and new risks. The students are always expected to join in, to prove their loyalty with public displays. The line between art and propaganda? It’s thin—and crossing it can be dangerous.
Even with all these challenges, the boy still finds moments of joy. A kind word from a teacher, nailing a performance, a letter from home—these small victories keep him going.
He starts to see that being resilient isn’t just about surviving hard times. It’s about finding meaning in the struggle itself.
The academy transforms him. He arrives as a child—uncertain, a little scared. But he leaves as a young man, shaped by discipline and ambition. The journey isn’t finished, not by a long shot, but the groundwork is set.
And those lessons—about grit, sacrifice, and the true power of art—will stick with him, guiding him through whatever comes next.
